author: Unknown
title: “How Has Serving Impacted You?” : Veterans of the US Military in Their Own Words
content:
What is it like to serve in the United States military? If only it were possible for those who are considering enlisting to learn the unvarnished truth. In 2019, a viral 

tweet

 from the official US Army twitter account unexpectedly drew over 11,000 candid replies in the course of 48 hours. These responses offer a rare window into the real experiences of servicemembers and veterans. We present a selection of them here for the benefit of anyone who is thinking about joining the military.




This is a document of an 

earlier era

 of social media, captured here before it 

vanishes

. You can obtain a book collecting the first twenty-four hours of responses 

here

.







Just before Memorial Day in 2019, the United States Army made a strategic blunder almost on par with invading Vietnam. They posted this inquiry on their official Twitter account:













In response, veterans and their family and friends posted thousands upon thousands of tweets recounting broken promises and broken people. They described cancer, PTSD, domestic abuse, unpaid college and housing loans, Gulf War syndrome, insomnia, sexual abuse, poverty, Agent Orange, racism, nightmare disorder, unemployment, burying loved ones, misogyny, orphaned children, burn pit syndrome, homelessness, debilitating injuries, divorce, alcoholism, disappearances, a Veterans Affairs department that was unwilling or unable to help, and suicide, suicide, suicide.








































































































































The United States military is one of the largest concentrations of power in the world. With 

tens of thousands

 of missiles, 

millions

 of firearms, and over 

5000

 nuclear weapons—about 40% of all the nuclear weapons in the world—the US military can hold the entire world hostage.





































The US military is also the largest employer in the United States, 

employing

 almost 2,900,000 workers—roughly 17 out of every 2000 people. If we add private military contractors like Blackwater (250,000 workers), the employees of non-combat support companies like Halliburton who build military infrastructure, provide food, and the like (150,000-250,000), US-based war manufacturers like Lockheed Martin and Boeing (1,500,000), and 

veterans

 who receive disability or pension payments (2,000,000), we find that roughly 1 out of every 50 Americans is economically dependent on US militarism.




As in all industries, without this workforce, the military would grind to a halt. It especially depends on regular transfusions of young blood—young people sold stories about adventure, duty, and upward mobility.





































If we were to ask new recruits why they joined, we’d 

likely

 hear a mix of narratives about gaining strength, seeing the world, paying for college, serving God and country, learning life skills, continuing a family tradition, escaping poverty or an unsafe home, obtaining housing, having fun, and protecting loved ones. Most people join the military because they think it will benefit them or because they believe they are serving a higher calling.














































Some recruits get to live out their dreams. Some leave instability, danger, or deprivation for a more structured and economically stable life; some even gain a sense of belonging. If they’re lucky, they serve their time without incident, then move on to free college tuition, a no-down-payment housing loan, health insurance, and a free meal at Golden Corral once a year.














































But thousands of veterans’ dreams become nightmares. The promises of recruiters, family members, and Hollywood movies offer a gamble at best—a roll of the dice that 

frequently

 ends with being harmed physically, psychologically, and sexually. Military service can lead to 

substance abuse

, 

homelessness

, and 

suicide

. It can also end in unspeakable acts of violence against others, whether those be the declared enemies of the United States, noncombatants, or veterans’ own loved ones.























































It is striking how many of these responses speak of being hoodwinked out of college, housing loans, and medical care—how many describe the pain of family members lost to PTSD, alcoholism, or suicide after witnessing or committing atrocities.














































American media bombards us with war propaganda. Almost every video game spreads the myth that combat makes us stronger: more powerful weapons, tougher armor, a bigger health bar, greater fortunes. Hollywood promises that the hero can weather any fight—or, if he can’t, his death will be meaningful and glorious.




Statistically speaking, the more we are exposed to combat, the more likely we are to be severely harmed, both physically and 

mentally

. This is true for both 

servicemembers

 and 

civilians

. As for the families we want to protect, at least 

one out of every three

 veterans brings the war home to their family through domestic abuse. Veterans are 

two to four times

 more likely to harm their families than their civilian counterparts.














































After massive troop and draftee 

resistance

 during the late 1960s and early 1970s, the US government ended selective compulsory military service (known as “the draft”). The military transitioned to a volunteer force, which means 

depending on

 recruits from families with a military tradition, working-class and impoverished enlistees, and whomever else recruiters can trick.




As one commenter pointed out,













How many people would give recruiters the time of day if they led with the truth?




“How would you like an 

11-20% chance

 of having debilitating PTSD? Or say, a 

7-11% chance

 of severe physical disability? A 32-50% chance you’ll 

physically

 or 

sexually

 abuse your family? If you’re a woman, I can promise you at least a 

25-50% chance

 that another service member will assault you. Or perhaps you’d like to become one of 

over 32,000 homeless veterans

?”




“But if you want to 

assault civilians

 in another country—to 

kill them and 

mutilate

 their bodies

—the likelihood of you getting in trouble will be 

almost zero.”














































If the benefits are bait to lure the young, the desperate, and the bored, what about the narratives that draw those who seek a higher calling?




Almost every war America has fought in the last hundred years has not achieved its stated goals. Supposedly, the US military invaded Iraq to bring stability, peace, and democracy to the region; in fact, it brought years of civil war and death. Most US citizens still cannot name the current Iraqi head of state or describe the political situation in Iraq. Twenty years of fighting in Afghanistan and Vietnam resulted in the Taliban and Việt Cộng acquiring more power than they started with. The Korean War has technically never ended; pick your poison—the poverty and hunger of a communist dictatorship or the sterility, inequality, and exploitation of the modern capitalist world.




We are told that World War II was fought to end authoritarianism and establish global peace. Yet fascism proper remained in power Spain and Portugal, while explicitly white supremacist governments retained control in places like South Africa—and the US government maintained supportive relations with all of them. In the wake of the war, humanity faced the threat of nuclear annihilation in a new Cold War. The military-industrial complex became one of the most powerful forces in society, and all kinds of violent and humiliating forms of oppression continued to exist in the victorious countries as well as the defeated ones.




But at least the Great War—the war fought to end all wars—brought lasting peace to the world. Right?























































War is a racket.

 The rich and powerful use those below them as cannon fodder as they maneuver to acquire more wealth and power. In 2003, the oil reserves of Iraq were the third largest in the world. Shortly after the US invasion and toppling of Saddam Hussein’s government, the reserves were privatized and contracted to Western companies, generating windfall profits for a few lucky capitalists.




A popular anti-war chant at the time exhorted, 

“ExxonMobil, BP, Shell, take your war and go to hell!”























































While militarists justified the War on Terror with rhetoric about fighting evildoers, the Bush administration sought to establish footholds on various continents in order to maintain military dominance throughout the world. One of the reasons the 

Afghan War

 lasted as long as it did is that the military industry prolonged it for profit. The United States government spent 

over $21,000,000,000,000

 on the War on Terror.




Weapons manufacturers made a killing. During the years 2020-2024 alone—in other words, well after the Iraq and Afghanistan wars were over—$771 billion
in Pentagon contracts 

went to

 Lockheed Martin ($313
billion), RTX (formerly Raytheon, $145 billion), Boeing ($115 billion), General Dynamics ($116 billion), and Northrop Grumman ($81 billion).
































































Even if we set aside the question of how the US government came to have $21 trillion at its disposal in the first place—think about what that $21 trillion spent on the War on Terror could have been used for instead. What do you need to live a happy, fulfilling life? What do the peoples of Iraq and Afghanistan and Vietnam need? How much healthcare and education could have been provided? Genuine healthcare, not what the VA and the for-profit hospitals crank out or deny. And real education—skills people need and want for life, knowledge based on our passions—not the traps that pass for schools in America, one part daycare and one part prison.




But thank goodness the US government didn’t go to the peoples of Iraq and Afghanistan and meet their needs. 

Fundamentalist extremism would surely have ballooned in popularity after that!























































It is not surprising that the US government and the warmongers didn’t meet the needs of the people they claimed to be liberating. They need new terrorists, or at least the threat of new terrorists, to keep up the racket. Without the fear of outsiders menacing America, how would they arrange trillions for war?





































We could tally up who profited on the Vietnam War or World War I with similar results. The protests and revolutions that broke out around the world during and after both of those wars indicate how millions of people understood what those wars were truly about. They showed successive generations that militarism, capitalism, nationalism, and authoritarianism only benefit those at the top.
































































Militarism always preys on the young and vulnerable, luring them with tales of heroism, riches, and duty. The young and desperate will serve their countries until they realize that their countries do not serve them.




No governments ever have. None ever will.





































The public can no longer view all of the replies to “How has serving impacted you?” The website still claims to retain 8.7k of them, but they are not accessible. In part, this is because people deleting their accounts, whether out of boredom with the platform or because they don’t want to support Elon Musk’s embrace of techno-fascism.




The X algorithm promotes conservative and extreme-right content, suppresses news from traditional corporate media outlets, and promotes “independent” but usually conservative or far-right influencers. When Elon Musk bought Twitter, he immediately 

purged

 high-profile accounts belonging to anarchists, anti-fascists, and far-left users. All of these are obstacles to using what remains of the platform under his ownership.





































In reaction to the neoconservatives in the Bush administration who led the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, many American conservatives shifted toward paleo-conservatism during the years-running Iraq and Afghanistan Wars. Some even became openly critical of war. Many believed that, in casting votes for Donald Trump, they were electing a politician who would keep the United States out of wars. But wherever there is nationalism, wherever state power is concentrated in the hands of an aspiring autocrat, 

war is never far behind

.




The answers to “How has serving impacted you?” comprise an interracial, multi-generational, gender-inclusive condemnation of the US military that cuts across the political spectrum. This is more of a liability to X’s brand of techno-fascism than an asset. Elon Musk’s platform has not buried them entirely, yet, but it’s not the sort of thing that he and his underlings would want people to easily and completely access. In view of that, it is unusual that so many damning tweets remain—a testament to how dangerous it is to trust your life to the military. It is worth documenting them before they disappear.




If you or your family members are currently serving in the US military, please contact the GI Rights Hotline at 1-877-447-4487 or just go AWOL. There is no need to stay in the service of a violent front for weapons and defense corporations. There’s no reason to die for their benefit, and there’s absolutely no excuse to become complicit in what the US government has done to to the people of Afghanistan, Iraq, and Iran.

title: The Hot Potato Changes Hands Again : On the 2026 Midterm Elections
content:
Ultimately, the Democrats are no more capable of addressing the root causes of popular anger than the Republicans. State power will continue to swing back and forth more and more wildly between different parties until our rulers consolidate an autocracy or we manage to effect revolutionary change.







As we anticipated 

in April

, the death knell of the Trump era has rung. Despite being 

historically unpopular

, Democratic politicians won a sweeping victory in the November 2026 midterm elections. Many are describing the rout as an “

extinction-level event

” for the Republican Party.




All this should feel familiar. Only two years ago, when Democrats lost the 2024 elections, pundits across the political spectrum rushed to declare the collapse of the Democratic Party. Summarizing a widespread perception, one 

expert

 claimed that







“Fundamental shifts are occurring in the body politic that have left Democrats on the wrong side of the popular vote, congressional races, and the country’s shifting demographics.”







Two years later, people are saying the same things about the Republican Party. The backlash against Republicans in this year’s election eclipses the gains they made in 2024. Yet the pendulum has been swinging wildly back and forth between parties for over a decade now—and it could be that the wildest swings have yet to come.




For all the talk of political polarization, loyalty to political parties is at its 

lowest

 in decades. Since at least 2016, anger at the status quo has been the most powerful force in politics; Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Joe Biden who attempted to present themselves as its defenders have learned that the hard way. Likewise, Donald Trump has only able to win elections when he is not in office. Whenever Trump represents the ruling order, he draws the same backlash that he once managed to channel.




Since 2014, we have argued that state power itself has become a hot potato that burns whoever holds it. In a globalized economy, in which governments can no longer mitigate the impact of capitalism on their citizens without investors taking their money elsewhere, no party is able to hold state power for long without losing credibility with voters. Similarly, the challenges of maintaining position as a waning imperial power inevitably undercut the legitimacy of whoever controls the state: just as the genocide in Gaza damaged the Biden administration’s support, Trump’s 

war with Iran

 has contributed to driving away voters.




Similar things are taking place all around the world. 

British politicians

 have also seen rapid reversals in fortune. The centrist parties that have long ruled Germany and France are in precipitous decline. One Latin American government after another has swung to the far right, but that hardly indicates a 

social consensus

 in favor of 

any political camp

.




Only countries under continuous autocratic rule, such as Russia, Belarus, China, and North Korea, are excepted from the hot potato pattern. Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to establish a similar state of affairs in the United States. Yet even in Hungary, which Republicans took as a model for their illiberal aspirations, the long-running autocratic government ultimately lost control. The same has occurred in Poland and, more recently, Serbia. Wherever voters have an opportunity—however narrow—to demand change, they do so—however arbitrarily and capriciously.




With no prospect of improving life for his rank-and-file supporters, Trump’s solution was to 

inflict violence

 on their behalf, offering them the vicarious thrill of watching the state cause harm to others as an outlet for their frustration. 

Less bread, more circuses

.







 




Republicans and Democrats—trash and recycling.










It might have worked—if ordinary people had not courageously taken the streets to interfere. We owe Trump’s failure to those who assembled at 

Tesla dealerships

 in spring 2025, who 

rose up

 against federal agents and the National Guard that June, who confronted Immigration and Customs Enforcement mercenaries in 

Chicago

, 

Minnesota

, and elsewhere. As we previously saw in 

the movement against police and white supremacy

, when people take risks in solidarity with others, this makes it possible for more people to experience empathy where previously, they only felt dissociation and apathy.




The grassroots resistance that emerged in response to the Trump administration stands in stark contrast to the way that elite figures across the political spectrum immediately put themselves as Trump’s disposal. Tech billionaires from Silicon Valley flocked to his inauguration to throw themselves at his feet. Powerful 

law firms

, university administrations, and 

corporations

 subordinated themselves to his will. Heads of state from across the world groveled and toadied to Trump—regardless of how he 

treated

 them, no matter how absurd his 

demands

.




Throughout 2025, Democratic politicians confined themselves to expressing opposition in purely symbolic ways, if occasionally 

at great length

. Cowardly centrist Democrats had already 

embraced Trump’s anti-immigrant politics

 well before the 2024 election; after it, many of them 

actively participated

 in the Trump regime’s attacks on immigrants, seizing the opportunity to call for the Democratic Party to continue tacking 

rightward

.




The scale of subsequent 

resistance

 to ICE showed that this was not hard-nosed pragmatism, but political opportunism at the service of xenophobia. A 

poll

 at the beginning of March 2026 showed that only 39% of respondents opposed abolishing ICE, with fully 50% actively calling for its abolition. The disparity between these figures and the very small number of politicians prepared to consider abolishing ICE even today shows that Democratic politicians will openly defy their supporters’ wishes in order to continue to advance a reactionary agenda. As politicians, they do not simply answer to a constituency of voters, but above all to a clientele of capitalists.




Trump did his best to rig the system in his favor ahead of the 2026 elections, arranging for widespread gerrymandering, seeking to control the voting process, and attempting to put the pieces in place to contest the results. Billionaires backed him financially—Elon Musk singlehandedly spent half a billion dollars, a quarter of the entire Republican budget for the election, in an effort to put his thumb on the scales. In the end, the results were so conclusive that none of this mattered. As in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the majority of voters rejected the reigning party.




Yet because this will was expressed via voting, rather than through more direct means, the result simply hands power to another coterie of politicians who will not address the needs of those who elected them. The more secure the Democrats’ grip on power becomes, the less they will concern themselves with the wishes of the electorate. If anything, the 2026 election will only embolden the centrists within the party, as it put power in the hands of more moderate Democrats, especially in swing districts.




But those who imagine that the Democrats did so well in the 2026 election on their own merits are fooling themselves.




The core issue at the root of the hot potato pattern is that the existing political order cannot address the instability, disparities, and crises of a capitalist system that has concentrated most of the wealth of society in the hands of a few while inflicting grievous social, psychological, and ecological damage on the rest of us. No political party will initiate the kind of revolutionary transformation that will be required to shift to a more egalitarian and sustainable way of life; such change can only come from grassroots mobilization. As long as there is no widespread, powerful social movement that offers the prospect of addressing these problems through profound change, people will continue rejecting one government after another in increasing desperation.




Silicon Valley tech moguls—who backed Joe Biden in 2020 only to switch sides in 2024—are even less popular than Donald Trump. Hatred of tech billionaires, data centers, and Flock cameras cuts across political lines; like the war on Iran, it is one of the factors that caused many former Trump voters to stay home or vote for Democrats. Yet as they regain their hold on power, Democrats will be inclined to work more and more closely with capitalists and the tech industry, rhetoric about “oligarchy” notwithstanding.













If social movements die down again as they did in 2021 after Biden took office, this will bode ill for the future, opening the way for even more extreme far-right reactionaries to pretend that they represent the only alternative to an unendurable status quo. If the 

cycle

 that played out between the first and second Trump administrations repeats itself again, the third iteration of far-right reaction will be more horrific than we can possibly imagine.




For good or ill, it does not look like anyone will be able to delude themselves into believing in a “return to normal” any time soon. The 

accession

 of Stephen Miller, an avowed white supremacist, to White House Chief of Staff sets the stage for the Trump administration to conclude with a period of brutal, open conflict. The administration lacks the support to win an open power struggle with the rest of society, but has left itself no alternative. As one 

New York Times

 commentator put it, “The next two years could actually be pretty volatile.”




As long as Trump remains in power, the far right will be perceived as the hegemonic force against which social anger will gravitate. But we must not wait for Democratic politicians to stand up to the Trump administration; even if they did, at best, that would function to relegitimize the same state institutions that will once again be turned against us in the future—as we saw in the Democrats’s response to the 

failed coup

 of January 6, 2021.




We must set an example by continuing to resist the Trump administration—and, wherever necessary, Democratic local and state administrations as well—through grassroots 

direct action

. Rather than simply waging a defensive struggle, we must figure out how to take proactive steps towards 

a completely different way of life

 in the process. Otherwise, the far right will eventually benefit once again from the inevitable disillusionment with Democratic administrations.




In short: it’s good to see Trump losing control. But the pendulum will continue to swing back and forth between political parties in wilder and wilder oscillations until we make revolutionary changes in our society.

content:
Helicopter hovering over Place de la République during the curfew implemented in Paris.

presidential election

 in May 2027, high school students have 

organized

 on a grassroots level. Through occupations, blockades, and street protests, they have taken a stand against both the deplorable conditions of their schools today and the 

menacing future

 that looms ahead of them. They took France and the entire world by surprise with their determined mass resistance and their courage in confronting the police forces sent to repress them.




After weeks of daily actions and nationwide demonstrations, leading to an unprecedented wave of arrests targeting rebellious youth, the Macron government was reaching a political impasse. It desperately tried to buy time by opening dialogue with some student organizations, in hopes of blunting the force of the movement until the upcoming school break slowed its momentum.

content:
Earlier this month, 

The Guardian

 

announced

 the existence of the 

NSPM-7 Defendants Union

, a new experiment in movement defense. We reached out to the organizers for an overview of their project, which we present here.







Announcing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union




National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7) is a government-wide strategy to investigate, disrupt, and prosecute what the Trump administration calls “left-wing political extremism.” They have already used it to justify publicly killing Minneapolis anti-ICE rapid responders Renee Good and Alex Pretti, 

raiding the homes

 of University of Michigan students protesting the genocide of Palestinians, and 

re-indicting

 Stop Cop City protesters.




But by the tens of thousands, newly politicized people are learning to fight: Minnesotan moms tracking BORTAC agents, students throwing back tear gas outside 

Delaney Hall

, nurses making split-decisions to help people escape from ICE. Especially in the movement against Trump’s deportation agenda, thousands of people are taking brave actions for the first time.

title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification : A Report from Madrid and Barcelona
content:
On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the 

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the 

Occupy

 movement in the United States.




Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.




Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.







 




Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.
